sources.headline: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
sources.text: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external. The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage."Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter."It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting. But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry."Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993. Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him. He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision. By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

sources.headline: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence
sources.text: Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

Published: 10:30pm, 9 Nov 2026Updated: 11:30pm, 9 Nov 2026

Nvidia is facing an unprecedented valuation test as a board inquiry into CEO Jensen Huang exposes the US chipmaker to a rare key-person risk, while investors also weigh the midterm elections’ potential impact on Washington’s chip controls and AI regulation.

The company’s shares slumped 7.3 per cent as markets opened in the United States on Monday, following Huang’s bombshell confirmation over the weekend that he had been unfaithful to his wife and would cooperate with an investigation into his conduct.

The probe has added to the turbulence facing the world’s largest chipmaker, whose shares endured a roller-coaster end to last week, tumbling 9.3 per cent on Thursday before rebounding 2.8 per cent on Friday.

The sudden convergence of shocks has also fuelled a counter-rally in Chinese alternatives, with shares of domestic chip designers surging in Shanghai on Monday on expectations that tightening US chip curbs could accelerate Beijing’s semiconductor self-reliance drive.

Cambricon Technologies and MetaX Integrated Circuits closed up 6.02 per cent and 5.66 per cent, respectively, while Enflame Technology soared 17.26 per cent.

The leadership scrutiny strikes at a vulnerable point for investors accustomed to Huang’s central role in Nvidia’s meteoric ascent.

“Investors tend to struggle to price in key-person and governance issues,” former Pimco CEO Mohamed El-Erian wrote in a social media post, pointing to Nvidia’s weight in global financial markets and the tech sector.

In a statement published on Sunday US time, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and would cooperate fully with the independent inquiry, which was opened after reports surfaced that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

Nvidia’s board expressed confidence in the CEO, saying it had no reason to believe that US national security or trade secrets had been compromised.

Compounding the turmoil are rising concerns over data-centre bottlenecks following last week’s US midterm elections. Democrats captured both chambers of Congress and flipped the governorship in Texas, a key hub for domestic AI infrastructure.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on pausing approvals for new data centre facilities until state lawmakers enact community-protection measures.

Wall Street has already begun pricing in infrastructure delays. In a client note on Sunday, Morgan Stanley analysts projected that 5 gigawatts of US data centre capacity originally forecast to come online in 2028 – about one-fifth of the total for that year – could be pushed to 2029 instead, citing likely postponements in Texas and Ohio.

At the same time, pressure is mounting in Washington to close loopholes in advanced semiconductor export-control regimes.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren said on CBS News on Sunday that there was bipartisan support on the Senate Banking Committee to enforce stricter curbs on chip shipments to China.

Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official and senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, also urged the US Department of Commerce to tighten export controls, arguing that existing regulations must be applied more rigorously to shipments routed through intermediaries in third-party jurisdictions.

Concerns over chip diversion have followed Nvidia for months. Culper Research, which disclosed a short position in the chipmaker in May, alleged that over 20 per cent of Nvidia’s compute revenue in its last financial year came from hidden Chinese demand routed through Southeast Asian intermediaries, including Singapore-based Megaspeed.

The New York Times reported in October that US officials had concluded Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive close to Jensen Huang, was passing information to Beijing.

Nvidia previously said that internal reviews found no evidence of Megaspeed diverting chips to China. Megaspeed and the Singapore authorities did not immediately respond to requests for comment from the South China Morning Post.

Beijing dismissed the allegations on Monday. “The ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular press briefing.

Nvidia, whose guidance for its October quarter assumed no data centre compute revenue from China, is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on November 17. The chairs of three US House committees have asked Huang to brief them behind closed doors on November 18.

Howard Liu
FOLLOW
Howard Liu is a Beijing-based technology and business reporter at the South China Morning Post, covering the semiconductor industry, AI and global tech supply chains. Previously at Caixin Media, he focused on China’s AI, semiconductor and cloud computing sectors. A graduate of Columbia University, he enjoys running, swimming and hiking.
